strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: existing methods for weight-space processing of neural fields (e.g., nf2vec) are strictly limited to fixed, specific neural architectures, whereas this work proposes an architecture-agnostic approach capable of processing varied and even unseen NeRF architectures.

The conceptual analysis of the latent space is insightful; the authors clearly demonstrate that a rendering reconstruction loss alone leads to undesirable architecture-based clustering, and show how a contrastive objective (SigLIP) successfully pulls equivalent representations of the same underlying 3D object together across architectures.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation covering multi-architecture classification, cross-architecture classification, unseen architecture generalization (varying MLP depths/widths and tri-plane resolutions/channels), and instance/class retrieval tasks.
The paper is well-written, clearly structured, and provides transparent discussion of limitations and failure cases.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is somewhat incremental, as the framework largely integrates existing components: the parameter graph conversion and GMN encoder from Lim et al. (2024), the conditioned NeRF decoder and rendering loss from nf2vec (Zama Ramirez et al., 2024), and the SigLIP loss formulation from Zhai et al. (2023).

Evaluation is restricted to synthetic ShapeNet objects and relatively small architectures (small 3-layer MLPs and low-resolution 32x32 tri-planes). State-of-the-art representations like multi-resolution hash encodings (Instant-NGP) or complex real-world scenes are not evaluated, which limits the immediate practical applicability.

High computational overhead and scalability concerns: converting neural networks into parameter graphs and running GNN message passing results in long training times (~2 weeks for small models on a single GPU) and low batch sizes (batch size 8), which may pose scalability bottlenecks for scaling up to larger architectures.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: previous weight-space representation learning methods for Neural Radiance Fields (e.g., nf2vec, Cardace et al.) are restricted to rigid, predefined architectures. This work takes a meaningful step toward architecture-agnostic neural field processing.

Insightful analysis of training objectives: the paper clearly demonstrates that rendering loss alone preserves architectural biases in the embedding space (forming separate clusters per architecture within each class), and convincingly demonstrates how contrastive alignment (SigLIP) mitigates this issue.

Thorough evaluation on zero-shot generalization across architectures: the authors test generalization to unseen network depths, hidden dimensions, tri-plane spatial resolutions, and channel counts, providing solid empirical evidence of robustness.
Well-structured and clearly presented paper with informative visualizations (t-SNE plots and retrieval qualitative examples) and transparent discussion of limitations.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to relatively small, simplified NeRF variants (3-layer MLPs and low-resolution 32x32 tri-planes on synthetic ShapeNet objects). While the authors acknowledge this limitation in Section 5, scaling to practical modern representations like multi-resolution hash encodings (Instant-NGP) or 3D Gaussian Splatting remains unaddressed.

The core technical components are largely compositions of existing techniques: the parameter graph conversion and GMN encoder are directly adapted from Lim et al. (2024), the auto-decoder from nf2vec (Zama Ramirez et al., 2024), and the contrastive loss from SigLIP (Zhai et al., 2023).

Computational scalability of the GMN encoder during training is a potential bottleneck (e.g., 2 weeks on an RTX 3090 for modest batch sizes and small NeRFs), which may hinder scaling to larger, scene-level radiance fields.

strengths: First framework to explore architecture-agnostic weight-space learning for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs), addressing a key limitation of existing weight-processing methods (such as nf2vec) that are restricted to rigid, predefined architectures.

Insightful analysis of the latent space geometry: clearly identifies and visualizes that rendering loss alone causes architecture-specific clustering within classes, and demonstrates that incorporating a contrastive loss (SigLIP) successfully bridges different parameterizations of the same underlying 3D content.

Comprehensive evaluation across multiple downstream settings, including single-architecture vs. multi-architecture classification, instance-level cross-architecture retrieval, and zero-shot transfer to unseen architectural variations (differing depth, width, and tri-plane resolution).
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the framework is largely an integration of existing components—the parameter graph conversion and Graph Meta-Network (GMN) architecture from Lim et al. (2024), the conditioned decoder and rendering loss from nf2vec (Zama Ramirez et al., 2024), and the standard SigLIP contrastive objective from Zhai et al. (2023).

Restricted architectural scope and scalability concerns: experiments are confined to small, simplified NeRF variants (3-layer MLPs and 32x32 low-resolution tri-planes). It remains unverified whether GMN parameter graphs can scale to modern, standard neural representations such as multiresolution hash grids (Instant-NGP) or higher-resolution 3D neural fields without prohibitive graph size and memory footprint during message passing.

Evaluation is limited strictly to synthetic 3D data (ShapeNetRender); evaluation on real-world NeRF captures (e.g., ScanNet or CO3D) is missing, leaving its practical utility on noisy or imperfect real-world reconstructions untested.

Modest performance on instance-level retrieval: while contrastive learning improves alignment, Table 5 shows Recall@1 on BOTH of only 29.0%, indicating that achieving true architectural invariance in weight space remains an open challenge.

strengths: Addresses an important and prominent limitation in neural field processing: prior weight-space representation methods (such as nf2vec and Cardace et al.) are strictly restricted to a single fixed architecture, whereas this work provides the first architecture-agnostic framework capable of ingesting diverse and unseen NeRF architectures.

Introduces an efficient parameter-graph formulation for multi-resolution hash tables that connects hash entries to feature dimensions, avoiding cubic scaling in resolution and enabling weight-space learning on hash-grid representations for the first time.

Presents an insightful latent space analysis demonstrating that rendering reconstruction losses alone lead to clustering by architecture modality rather than semantic content, and effectively resolves this via a multi-architecture contrastive objective (SigLIP).

Thorough empirical evaluation across 13 architectures spanning three distinct architectural families (MLPs, tri-planes, hash tables), demonstrating strong cross-architecture transfer, robust generalization to unseen architectures, and competitive performance against single-architecture baselines.
weaknesses: High computational cost and limited architectural scale: pre-training takes approximately two weeks on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 with a small batch size (B=8). Consequently, the evaluated NeRFs are restricted to compact scales (e.g., hash tables of size 2^11-2^12 and small MLPs with width 32-64), which are substantially smaller than typical full-scale Instant-NGP or NeRF configurations.

Absolute retrieval precision across disparate architecture pairs remains relatively modest in terms of Recall@1 (e.g., Table 6 shows Recall@1 under 15% for several cross-architecture pairs like MLP/HASH and HASH/TRI), indicating room for improvement in fine-grained alignment.

Experiments are largely confined to synthetic, object-centric ShapeNet models without view-dependent effects (simplified coordinate-to-color/density mapping), leaving the behavior on real-world forward-facing or unbounded 360-degree scenes unverified.

strengths: First architecture-agnostic framework for NeRF weight-space representation learning: unlike prior works (e.g., nf2vec, Cardace et al.) which are strictly limited to fixed MLPs or fixed-resolution tri-planes, this paper successfully handles diverse NeRF architectures and even generalizes to unseen architectural configurations at test time.

Novel graph parameterization for multi-resolution hash encodings: the paper proposes an efficient parameter graph formulation for Instant-NGP-style hash tables that avoids cubic scaling with voxel resolution by mapping table entries and feature dimensions directly.

Insightful analysis of the loss formulation: the authors show convincingly (both via t-SNE latent space analysis and downstream experiments) that rendering loss alone causes distinct clustering by architecture type, whereas incorporating a SigLIP-based contrastive loss is critical to enforce architecture-invariance.

Extensive experimental evaluation: the empirical study evaluates 13 distinct architectures across three architectural families (MLPs, tri-planes, and hash tables), assessing both matched and cross-architecture classification, unseen architectural variations, and instance-level cross-architecture retrieval.
Strong paper clarity and organization: the methodology, architecture conversions, and trade-offs between rendering and contrastive objectives are clearly described and well-motivated.
weaknesses: Instance retrieval across the unified pool remains challenging: as shown in Table 6, Recall@1 for the ALL/ALL setting is relatively low (5.3%), and Recall@10 is 27.2%, indicating that achieving full instance-level alignment across all three disparate architecture families simultaneously is difficult.

Evaluation is predominantly confined to synthetic ShapeNet models: while an Objaverse qualitative evaluation is included, the quantitative benchmarking is limited to ShapeNetRender; evaluating on real-world forward-facing or 360-degree scenes would provide stronger evidence of broader applicability.

Sensitivity to specific architectural shifts: the framework demonstrates significant performance degradation on certain unseen hyperparameter shifts, notably changes in hash table size (e.g., HASH-11T in Tables 4 and 5 drops classification accuracy to ~25-29%), indicating that parameter graphs remain partially sensitive to structural scaling.

Computational overhead: due to large parameter graphs and message-passing iterations, training takes approximately two weeks on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 with a small batch size of 8, which may hinder scaling to larger foundation-scale meta-networks.

strengths: First framework capable of performing weight-space representation learning across diverse and heterogeneous NeRF architectures (MLPs, tri-planes, and multi-resolution hash grids).

Novel and scalable parameter graph construction for multi-resolution hash encodings, which avoids memory-prohibitive dense voxel grid representations by connecting hash entry nodes to feature dimension nodes.

Insightful analysis and ablation of the loss formulations (rendering loss vs. contrastive SigLIP loss vs. combined), clearly demonstrating that rendering loss alone causes architecture-specific clustering while contrastive alignment promotes architectural invariance.

Thorough empirical evaluation across 13 distinct architectures, including rigorous out-of-distribution evaluation on 10 unseen architectures differing in layer depth, feature width, plane resolution, and hash table capacity.
Strong competitive performance in single-architecture setups, matching or exceeding specialized prior methods such as nf2vec and Cardace et al.
weaknesses: Limited dataset diversity: the quantitative evaluation is restricted to synthetic, object-centric ShapeNetRender models across 13 classes, with real-world or unbounded complex scenes unaddressed.

Absolute retrieval performance remains low: cross-architecture instance retrieval yields modest Recall@1 scores (e.g., 5.3% on ALL/ALL and 9.5%–33.3% across cross-architecture pairs), indicating that fine-grained instance alignment across disparate parameterizations remains challenging.

The parameter graph formulation for hash tables discards explicit spatial neighborhood topology (unlike the tri-plane graph where spatial positions are explicitly encoded as edge features), which may hinder geometric transfer across different grid resolutions.
High training computational cost: end-to-end training of the GNN encoder alongside volumetric rendering requires approximately two weeks on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU for a moderate batch size of 8.

Downstream tasks are limited to basic classification and nearest-neighbor retrieval; evaluating representation utility on generative modeling, NeRF editing, or view interpolation would strengthen the significance.
